blocks.text: K. stared at the inspector. Was he to be given schoolroom lessons here by a person who was perhaps younger than himself? Was he to be punished with a reprimand for his frankness? And about the reason for his arrest and about who had ordered it he was to learn nothing?

He grew somewhat agitated, walked up and down, which no one prevented him from doing, pushed back his cuffs, felt his chest, smoothed his hair, passed by the three gentlemen, said, "It's senseless, though," whereupon they turned round to him and looked at him obligingly but gravely, and finally came to a halt again before the inspector's table. "Public Prosecutor Hasterer is a good friend of mine," he said, "may I telephone him?" "Certainly," said the inspector, "but I don't know what sense there would be in that, unless it were that you had some private matter to discuss with him." "What sense?" cried K., more dismayed than annoyed. "Who are you, then? You want sense, and you are staging the most senseless thing there is. Isn't it enough to make the stones weep? These gentlemen first fell upon me, and now they sit or stand about here and make me perform haute école before you. What sense there would be in telephoning a public prosecutor when I am supposedly under arrest? Very well, I shall not telephone." "But do," said the inspector, stretching out his hand toward the anteroom, where the telephone was, "please, do telephone." "No, I no longer want to," said K., and went to the window. Across the way the party was still at the window and seemed only now, by K.'s having stepped up to the window, to be somewhat disturbed in the calm of their watching. The old people wanted to get up, but the man behind them calmed them. "There are spectators like that over there too," K. called out quite loudly to the inspector, pointing outside with his forefinger. "Away from there," he then called across. The three did at once retreat a few steps, the two old people even behind the man, who shielded them with his broad body and, to judge by the movements of his mouth, said something that was unintelligible at that distance. But they did not disappear entirely; rather they seemed to be waiting for the moment when they might approach the window again unnoticed. "Importunate, inconsiderate people!" said K., as he turned back into the room. The inspector possibly agreed with him, as K. believed he could see with a sidelong glance. But it was just as possible that he had not been listening at all, for he had pressed one hand firmly on the table and seemed to be comparing the lengths of his fingers. The two guards sat on a trunk covered with an ornamental cloth and rubbed their knees. The three young men had put their hands on their hips and were looking around aimlessly. It was as quiet as in some forgotten office. "Well, gentlemen," cried K., and for a moment it seemed to him as if he were carrying them all on his shoulders, "judging by your appearance, my affair must be at an end. I am of the opinion that it is best to reflect no further on whether your proceedings were justified or unjustified, and to bring the matter to a conciliatory close with a mutual handshake. If you too are of my opinion, then please—" and he stepped up to the inspector's table and held out his hand to him. The inspector raised his eyes, gnawed at his lips and looked at K.'s outstretched hand; K. still believed the inspector would take it. But he stood up, took a hard round hat that lay on Fräulein Bürstner's bed and carefully put it on with both hands, as one does when trying on new hats. "How simple everything seems to you!" he said to K. as he did so, "we ought to bring the matter to a conciliatory close, did you say? No, no, that really won't do. By which, on the other hand, I by no means wish to say that you should despair. No, why should you? You are only under arrest, nothing more. That is what I had to inform you of; I have done so and have also seen how you have taken it. That is enough for today and we can take our leave, though only for the time being. I suppose you will want to go to the bank now?" "To the bank?" asked K., "I thought I was under arrest." K. asked with a certain defiance, for although his handshake had not been accepted, he felt, especially since the inspector had stood up, more and more independent of all these people. He was playing with them. He intended, should they leave, to run after them as far as the front door and offer them his arrest. That was why he repeated: "How can I go to the bank, then, since I am under arrest?" "Ah, I see," said the inspector, who was already at the door, "you have misunderstood me. You are under arrest, certainly, but that is not to prevent you from carrying on your profession. Nor are you to be hindered in your ordinary way of life." "Then being under arrest is not so very bad," said K., and went up close to the inspector. "I never meant otherwise," said the latter. "But then it seems that not even the notification of the arrest was very necessary," said K., and went closer still. The others too had drawn nearer. They were all now gathered in a narrow space by the door. "It was my duty," said the inspector. "A stupid duty," said K. unyieldingly. "That may be," answered the inspector, "but we don't want to waste our time with such talk. I had assumed that you would want to go to the bank. Since you pay attention to every word, I will add: I am not forcing you to go to the bank, I had only assumed that you would want to. And to make that easier for you, and to make your arrival at the bank as inconspicuous as possible, I have kept these three gentlemen, your colleagues, here at your disposal." "What?" cried K., and stared at the three in astonishment. These so uncharacteristic, anaemic young men, whom he still remembered only as a group by the photographs, were in fact officials from his bank, not colleagues, that was saying too much and already a gap in the inspector's omniscience, but subordinate officials from the bank they certainly were. How could K. have overlooked that? How absorbed he must have been by the inspector and the guards not to recognize these three. The stiff Rabensteiner, swinging his hands, the blond Kullich with the deep-set eyes, and Kaminer with his insufferable smile, caused by a chronic muscle strain, "Good morning!" said K. after a little while and held out his hand to the gentlemen, who bowed correctly. "I didn't recognize you at all. Well then, we shall go to work now, shall we?" The gentlemen nodded, laughing and eager, as if they had been waiting for this the whole time; only when K. missed his hat, which had been left lying in his room, did they all run one behind the other to fetch it, which did after all suggest a certain embarrassment. K. stood still and watched them through the two open doors; the last, naturally, was the indifferent Rabensteiner, who had merely broken into an elegant trot. Kaminer handed over the hat, and K. had to tell himself expressly, as was in fact often necessary at the bank too, that Kaminer's smile was not intentional, indeed that he could not smile intentionally at all. In the anteroom Frau Grubach, who did not look at all very guilty, then opened the apartment door for the whole party, and K. looked down, as so often, at her apron string, which cut so unnecessarily deep into her massive body. Downstairs K., watch in hand, decided to take a motor-car, so as not to increase unnecessarily his delay, which already amounted to half an hour. Kaminer ran to the corner to fetch the car, the two others were evidently trying to divert K., when suddenly Kullich pointed to the front door of the house opposite, in which the tall man with the blond pointed beard had just appeared and, in the first moment a little embarrassed at now showing himself at his full height, stepped back to the wall and leaned against it. The old people were probably still on the stairs. K. was annoyed with Kullich for drawing attention to the man, whom he himself had already seen earlier, indeed whom he had even expected. "Don't look over there," he blurted out, without noticing how striking such a manner of speaking was toward independent men. But no explanation was necessary either, for just then the motor-car came, they got in and drove off. Then K. remembered that he had not noticed the inspector and the guards leaving at all; the inspector had hidden the three officials from him, and now the officials had hidden the inspector. That did not show much presence of mind, and K. resolved to observe himself more closely in this respect. Yet he still turned round involuntarily and leaned forward over the rear deck of the motor-car, in order possibly still to see the inspector and the guards. But at once he turned back again and leaned comfortably into the corner of the car without having made even the attempt to look for anyone. Although it did not appear so, he would have needed encouragement just now, but now the gentlemen seemed tired, Rabensteiner looked out of the car to the right, Kullich to the left, and only Kaminer was at his disposal with his grin, about which, unfortunately, humanity forbade making a joke.
